#2619. MLB rumors: Yankees moves heating up, plus latest on Tarik Skubal, Mets, Padres, Red Sox, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near-certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free-agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Friday's supply just below.

The buzz at the GM Meetings last week was that the Mets offered top free agent Tarik Skubal a nine-year contract worth almost $400 million, reports MLB Network Radio. If the deal is worth at least $390 million, it would set new records for total guarantee and average annual value given to a pitcher. Here are the current pitcher contract records:

Given the player and the deep-pocketed teams involved in the bidding (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), Skubal is well-positioned to shatter Yamamoto's record. He could beat Scherzer's and Verlander's record as well. The expected lockout will begin after the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Skubal is likely to sign before then.

The Diamondbacks are set to acquire righty Johan Oviedo from the Red Sox for minor-league lefty Luke Dotson and a player to be named later, reports the Arizona Republic. Boston had four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Oviedo, Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck) and always seemed likely to trade one to ease the logjam.

Acquired from the Pirates last offseason, Oviedo made just one ineffective appearance around elbow trouble in 2026. He returned from Tommy John surgery in 2025 and looked excellent, and Arizona will hope Oviedo rediscovers that magic as he gets further away from his injuries. Dotson is not a top prospect. It's a low-cost flier for the D-backs.

The Tigers have signed right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year extension worth $46.5 million, reports ESPN. There is a club option for a seventh year and escalators can push the total guarantee to $80 million. Melton still had five years of team control. The new extension buys out his five team control years and one free agent year with an option for another free agent year.

Melton, 26 next month, missed the start of the season with elbow inflammation and finished the season on the injured list with more elbow woes. Between injuries, he made 20 starts with a sub-3.00 ERA with strong under-the-hood numbers. The Tigers know him better than anyone and are obviously comfortable with Melton's medicals to lock him up long-term.

The New York Yankees have agreed to a two-year contract with veteran right-hander Jonathan Loáisiga, ESPN reports. The deal also includes a club option for 2029 and is worth roughly $18 million, according to MLB.com.

Loáisiga, 32, is coming off that strong season above for the Arizona Diamondbacks, and for his career boasts an ERA+ of 128 across parts of nine MLB seasons. He's worked in relief for almost all of that span, and eight of those nine seasons came with the Yankees.

New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman was recently asked if he'd be willing to play Spencer Jones in center field. In response, he told media, including SNY, this:

"I would be comfortable with that. At the same time Jasson Domínguez is pounding the ball in winter ball. The entire industry is noticing that based on the phone calls I'm getting."

The 23-year-old Domínguez still has big-time power potential, and defensively he's best suited to center field. For his career in the Bronx, he has an OPS+ of 93, but his 751 plate appearances have been doled out erratically across four seasons. As things stand now, he'll once again be subject to a playing-time crunch. Aaron Judge and Cody Bellinger are installed at the outfield corners, and Giancarlo Stanton, if healthy, should get much of the playing time at DH. That leaves center field for Jones or Domínguez. Other teams no doubt see that bottleneck and are seeing if Cashman and the Yankees are willing to relieve it through trade.

Lefty ace and two-time American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal remains far and away the top talent on the free-agent market. While the New York Mets and incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers seem like the favorites to secure his services, the San Diego Padres also have significant interest in him. That interest took the next step on Thursday with an in-person meeting, The Athletic reports. The Padres are the fourth team to meet with Skubal, who turned 30 on Friday. Previously, the Dodgers, Mets, and Toronto Blue Jays met with him.

The Padres have a pronounced need in the rotation, especially if free-agent right-hander Michael King signs elsewhere. Last winter, they also lost Dylan Cease to the Blue Jays via free agency.

The Padres and left-handed platoon hitter Gavin Sheets have agreed to a three-year, $11 million contract extension that includes two opt-outs, FanSided reports. Sheets, who'll turn 31 in April, had been slated for free agency after the upcoming season. Instead, he and the Padres will now be potentially committed through the 2029 season, depending on whether Sheets exercises any of his opt-outs. While he's not much of a hitter for average, he does draw walks and hit for power. In two seasons with San Diego, he's tallied 36 home runs and 44 doubles in 855 at-bats while seeing DH, first base, and the outfield corners.

The New York Mets have agreed to a three-year, $12 million deal with right-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández, reports José F. Rivera.

Hernández, who turns 30 in December, hasn't pitched in MLB since 2022 and instead has revived his career with four strong seasons in Japan. Over that span for Softbank of the NPB, he's put up an ERA of 2.46 in 131 ⅔ innings with 168 strikeouts and 42 unintentional walks. Prior to rebuilding himself in Japan, Hernández had a 5.06 ERA and a 1.82 K/BB ratio over parts of four seasons with the Boston Red Sox.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2617. Jerry Jones defends Mike McCarthy's Cowboys tenure after Aaron Rodgers claims

Jerry Jones had plenty to reflect upon after the Dallas Cowboys lost to the Philadelphia Eagles 39-38 on Thanksgiving Day Thursday, Nov. 26.

Speaking to reporters after the loss, Jones said he wanted to keep former head coach Mike McCarthy an additional season after his five-year contract expired after 2024. McCarthy, now in his first season coaching the Pittsburgh Steelers, was replaced by Brian Schottenheimer.

"I offered him to stay at least another year when he left," Jones told reporters. "And so I thought he was outstanding as the head coach and had a great command of, frankly, (the) quarterback, (the) offense. (I) can't say enough good things about him. He's, frankly, one of the finest people around football that I've been around. And I can't say enough about him. I never had the type of thing that is being said about him. I never had that in consideration in any of my time with him, extending his contract. Any of that, that was never on the table. And we never had an issue within the organization."

A day earlier, now former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings and skipping practices this season and in the past, dating back to the quarterback-head coach pairing's with the Green Bay Packers from 2008 to 2018. Rodgers said McCarthy recently broke down a halftime huddle with "3, 2, 1 ... Packers," which prompted the quarterback to go scorched earth during an interview with "The Pat McAfee Show." The Steelers released Rodgers later in the day and he cleared waivers Thursday. (McCarthy did not deny the incident.)

In five seasons with the Cowboys, McCarthy missed the playoffs in his first and final seasons but rattled off three consecutive 12-5 campaigns that resulted in playoff berths. However, his team was 1-3 in the postseason.

McCarthy and the Steelers are playing the "Black Friday" game Nov. 27 at 3 p.m. ET against the Denver Broncos.

#2616. Game Preview #20: Wolves vs Grizzlies Game Thread

Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. As your holiday winds down, I'm pleased to bring you a brief preview of the next Minnesota Timberwolves game, which is against the Memphis Grizzlies.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (14-5) at Memphis Grizzlies (14-5)

This matchup will be the final game of the group stage for the NBA Cup, and the winner will get an automatic place in the cup playoffs. The Wolves have yet to reach that stage of the tournament, so putting together a win to make it there would be yet another great chapter within the storybook of this resurgent season.

A loss would not be ideal, though it would not be the end of the world as far as the Cup is concerned. Minnesota is in a pretty good position to make it in as a wildcard team over the Denver Nuggets based upon point differential. Obviously winning any game is the best-case scenario, though the Wolves have multiple paths towards competing for the increasingly-coveted NBA Cup title.

Regardless of Cup implications, this should be yet another good matchup between two teams that have been consistently strong in the Western Conference. Minnesota took the last matchup at home 104-95 which featured strong performances from Jaden McDaniels, Ayo Dosunmu, Jonathan Kuminga, and Terrence Shannon Jr. The Wolves will need to keep up their positive momentum from all of those guys if they look to clinch the group and pass the Grizzlies in the Western Conference standings.

That said, it may still be tough sledding for an already-injured team that may be dealing with another one for the foreseeable future. Keeping that in mind, here are a couple things I'm looking for in the game tomorrow:

Watching LaMelo Ball gingerly limp off of the court against the Oklahoma City Thunder was not a welcome sight. We got the win, but everyone is hoping that his turned ankle does not turn out (pun intended) to be anything serious.

It would not be out of the realm of possibility for Ball to miss this game. However, the team that used to boast significant guard depth is looking considerably weaker if we have the quadrio of Ball, Anthony Edwards, Donte DiVincenzo, and Jaylen Clark all sidelined.

As it were, this means that Bones Hyland should get a sizable helping of playing time. I would not be shocked to see G-League stud Zyon Pullin also get a fair bit of run to ease what would otherwise be a hefty serving of minutes for Hyland and Dosunmu. We've learned this season just how important adequate point guard play is with the addition of Ball, and I do not think Chris Finch would overwork the two guards left that are capable of stuffing that position.

On the other side of the scorer's table, the Grizzlies also have their share of injuries to deal with. Rookie forward Cameron Boozer is still out with injury, and Zach Edey is a game time decision after picking up a knock in their last game against the Los Angeles Clippers. With Jerami Grant, GG Jackson, and Scottie Pippen Jr. all still on the injured list as well, Memphis has had plenty of guys step up and give the team quality minutes in their absences. They may need more help if they are looking to defeat the Wolves on Friday.

What can't Jaden McDaniels do? Nothing, apparently. The guy has been a machine as of late, averaging 26 points per game while shooting the ball well over 67% from the floor and 69% from deep across his last five games. Those are some nice numbers.

On top of that, Jaden is continuing to put the clamps on opposing teams' best players. He locked up Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at the end of the game last evening, and McDaniels never appears to tire across the course of the game. He's doing it all for the Timberwolves, and that production has been necessary in the wake of the Edwards injury.

There is a legitimate argument to be made regarding Jaden as an All Star candidate this season. That argument will be bolstered if he can continue to control games with Ball sidelined. It's not McDaniels's fault that he is in this position to carry the team on his back, though his admirable performances are earning attention league-wide.

Next man up is always the mentality, and Jaden has been doing his part in keeping this injury-addled team afloat. Adding another injury to that mix certainly changes the dynamic of the team, though McDaniels has been playing strong enough that he should be able to overcome the absence of Ball.

I've mentioned in past articles that while Ball hasn't had the most statistical significance across the last couple weeks, he is unquestionably controlling the game and making the offense easier for everyone else. With him out, someone else will have to step up to make some shots and draw the defense in their direction. That person should be Terrence Shannon Jr.

He's had a few up-and-down performances lately, and his last game against the Thunder saw him score only eight points on 2/10 shooting while turning the ball over three times. Minnesota won the game, but they will need more production out of TJ with Ball being out against a tough opponent in Memphis.

A brief positive for TJ could be conceptualized with the news of Ball's absence, as the ball will likely be in the hands of Shannon more during his minutes. Last year gave the film buffs tons of evidence about how effective TJ can be as a scorer if he is initiating the offense. If he has more opportunity to control the lineups when he is deployed, he should be able to find a rhythm quickly.

Efficient scoring performances from TJ are always welcome sights. He has already been an integral part of this team with the current injury situation, and that importance will be inflated with yet another injury to a key player that plays heavy minutes. Expect Finch to lean on Shannon early and often in this contest.

This one is going to be a nail-biter, but I can't bet against the Wolves no matter who we play against. Expect TSJ to have a strong scoring night and, ideally, a grand re-opening of the Bone Zone. I think the Wolves take this one, but not by much.

#2614. Luis Gil, Nolan Gorman, Trevor Larnach, more hit MLB free agency after non-tender deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Friday marked the non-tender deadline in Major League Baseball. That important date on the offseason calendar is when clubs must make, or "tender," contract offers for the upcoming season to all their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on the 40-player roster. That's every player who isn't a free agent or isn't presently signed to a multi-year contract. Players who are tendered a contract by that deadline remain with their current organizations. Players who aren't offered a contract become free agents.

Most such decisions are easy and obvious. Others, however, present difficult calls for the organization because of roster crunches, crowded depth charts, or, more commonly, reluctance to retain a player as his salary rises through the arbitration process. While a number of non-tendered players are likely on their way out of the league, a select few others qualify as at least interesting to other teams and, on occasion, a few will even be coveted to varying degrees.

All that sets the stage for what follows, which is our list of the most compelling non-tendered players who are now on the market and available for hire. Let's get to it …

The 2024 AL Rookie of the Year, Gil has been injured and ineffective the last two seasons. He missed time with a shoulder issue this past season and also spent time in Triple-A. The Yankees moved him to the bullpen late in the season to see whether he could contribute that way, though Gil was unable to make a strong impression in that role. Now 28, Gil still has another three seasons of team control remaining. Whichever team signs him will be able to keep him through 2029, and that extra control, plus his Rookie of the Year pedigree, will no doubt land Gil with a new team before Opening Day.

As a 23-year-old in 2023, the infielder and former first-rounder hit 27 home runs in 119 games and looked like a future cornerstone for the Cardinals. Gorman, however, has gotten steadily worse since then thanks largely to his persistent strikeout issues. Last season, he wound up back at Triple-A for an extended stretch and didn't fare any better upon being recalled. Long-term, the Cardinals will likely look to hand the third base position to rising power prospect Jesús Báez, who was recently added to the 40-player roster. Gorman can be a plus at third and probably still get by at second, and no doubt some team will take a chance on his power.

On the downside, Larnach is a defensive minus at the corner outfield spots and probably needs to be a DH, and he's also a platoon bat. On the upside, he's been a steady producer from the left side of the plate. This past season, he put up a .352 OBP and an OPS+ of 120 for Minnesota. For his career, he has an OPS+ of 106 across parts of six MLB seasons. He out-hit his underlying indicators by a bit in 2026, but Larnach is still going to be an appealing part-time bat for some teams.

The Twins cut bait on a right-hander who's made 139 career starts for them since his 2021 big-league debut. Ober boasts a career OPS+ of 102, but that figure has slid over the last two seasons. What's also slid is Ober's fastball velocity, which may be why he's on this list. In his rookie season, he averaged a fringy 92.4 mph with his four-seamer, but last season that figure was down all the way to 88 mph. That put him in the very bottom percentile among MLB hurlers. The 31-year-old Ober still should draw some interest as a depth piece.

A platoon extraordinaire, Raley has always hit for power against righties, including 15 home runs in only 290 plate appearances against them in 2026. He's sneaky fast and a very good athlete for his size (6-foot-3 and 235 lbs.), good enough to handle the corner outfield spots competently. Raley also has first base experience and can patrol center field in a pinch. The Mariners cut him loose even though he will remain under team control through 2028. Raley's power against righties and an extra year of control could make him a solid bench option moving forward.

#2612. Andy Reid disagrees with overturned Rashee Rice catch after Chiefs' loss to Bills: 'That was not clear and obvious'

Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice appeared to have a much-needed first down against the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving. The NFL's replay center disagreed.

With the game tied 10-10 and two minutes left in the fourth quarter, the Chiefs got the ball deep in their own territory. A pair of incompletions left them facing third-and-10, at which point Patrick Mahomes appeared to connect with wide receiver Rashee Rice for 11 yards and the first down.

However, the play was surprisingly overturned on replay, with the official only saying, "After review, the ball hit the ground, it's an incomplete pass."

The call was popular at Buffalo's Highmark Stadium, but not so much on social media.

The video replay indeed showed the ball hit the ground while pinned between Rice's right hand and shoulder, but that alone doesn't make the play an incomplete pass. The ball must also come loose while hitting the ground before Rice establishes possession, and that was very much up for debate.

Additionally, the NFL maintains a "clear and obvious" standard for overturning plays. So the replay officials in New York City not only believed Rice hadn't completed the catch, they also decided it was clear to anyone watching.

Chiefs head coach Andy Reid very much didn't seem to think that was the case after his team's 13-10 defeat, via Kansas City's KSHB 41:

"Not [a call] that I agreed with, but yeah. This came from New York, so it's not from these guys. Our guys called it a completion, the guys who were working the game. I'm not quite sure what they saw. I saw he had control of the ball and his elbow hit and then the ball hit, but he had control.

"Normally, in those kind of situations, it's gotta be clear and obvious. To me, that was not clear and obvious."

Rashee Rice appeared to have a first down for the Chiefs. The NFL's replay center disagreed.

Mahomes' wife Brittany, meanwhile, used the occasion to dispute the idea the Chiefs have benefited from calls during their recent run, writing the following on her Instagram story:

"Guess we can't even play football without getting it called against us… not sure what an actual catch is after that I guess? I don't wanna hear s*** anymore from anyone"

She also posted a collection of social media posts criticizing the call to her story.

NFL vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth spoke to a pool reporter, pointing to Rice's hand moving up the ball as evidence that he lost control.

To be clear, this play did not singlehandedly cost the Chiefs the game, though it's undeniably frustrating. Had the Rice catch stood, they still would have needed to travel half the field to reach field-goal range, on a day in which struggling kicker Harrison Butker made one field goal from 26 yards and missed another from 46.

Facing fourth-and-10, Kansas City was instead forced to punt out of its own end zone. The teams immediately exchanged three-and-outs and appeared headed to overtime, only for field position to bite the Chiefs again when a disastrous punt sequence put the Bills in field-goal position for the final play.

#2611. Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations rules between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.

Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"

Sheikh Mansour's control of Manchester City has come into question [Getty Images]

When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."

Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football £20.3m annually.

Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

The IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

City have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

#2610. Melton hit 8 threes on Kings, joined an exclusive Warriors’ club

De'Anthony Melton nailed eight threes against Sacramento on Wednesday night and sent me down a rabbit hole (brought to you by Stathead) that ate up a lot more of my Thanksgiving than I planned.

Melton tied his career high with eight threes and scored 24 points in the 129-110 NBA Cup win over the Kings, and he did it with Steph sitting out with a torn oblique. He went 8-for-12 from deep, 8-for-14 overall, and never took a free throw.

With those eight treys, Melton walked into one of the most exclusive shooting clubs in franchise history. All of which got me wondering how often the Warriors lose when somebody does that. The answer is: almost never.

Since Coach Steve Kerr took over in 2014, there have been 120 regular-season performances where a Warrior hit eight or more threes, spread across 119 games because Curry and Wiggins share one, and the Warriors are 92-27 in those games. That's a .773 winning percentage, a 63-win pace, and the average scoring margin across all 119 games, wins and losses together, is almost plus-10.

Melton is the eighth different Warrior to do it under Kerr. The other seven are Curry, Klay Thompson, D'Angelo Russell, Jordan Poole, Wiggins, Brandin Podziemski and Moses Moody, and if you squint, that list doubles as a decade of Warriors history.

By the way, if I told you two Warriors once hit eight threes apiece in the same game during the Steve Kerr era would you bet on that being the Splash Brothers? Wrong, dear reader. Twas' Curry and Andrew Wiggins.

But let's find some more fun facts. During the first five seasons of the Kerr era, 2014-15 through 2018-19, the Warriors went 50-4 when somebody hit eight threes. Since then they're 42-23. A 92.6% winning percentage turned into 64.6%. Remember when Steph would hit his sixth three and you'd start figuring out how to beat the traffic out of Oracle? Nowadays a sixth three means you're hoping the Warriors can get a stop at the other end.

In the 73-9 season they went 20-1 in these games, which means somebody hit eight threes in roughly one out of every four games that year. The one loss took history to pull off. On April 1, 2016, Curry hit eight threes against Boston and the Celtics still won 109-106, ending the 54-game home winning streak, an NBA record. Even the losses from that era came with a plaque.

Those dynasty teams had the defense, depth and talent to turn a hot shooting night into an early bedtime for everybody watching on the East Coast.

Curry has 88 of the 120 performances, and Steph and Klay have a combined 111 of them, 92.5% of the entire club. The Warriors are 68-20 when Steph hits eight. Through age 34, the Warriors were 56-10 in his eight-three games. Since he turned 35, they're 12-10. Since he turned 37, they're 3-3.

He's still having these nights, and that's what gets me. In January 2025, at 36, he went 8-for-8 from three against Philadelphia, the only perfect night in the entire dataset. He dropped 31 with eight threes on the Lakers a month ago at 38 years old. The miracle nights keep coming, but they used to be a guaranteed win and now they're closer to a coin flip. The worst one to look back on is February 2024 in Atlanta, when he scored 60 with 10 threes and lost in overtime. He's lost 57-point and 50-point games too. The Warriors are 10-3 when Curry scores at least 50 points and makes at least eight threes, and they went 4-0 when Klay did it. When Steph has gone nuclear lately, he's usually been making up for everything around him.

Across his whole Warriors run under Kerr, 2014-15 through 2023-24, Klay went 19-4 in his eight-three games and 13-1 at home. He scored 60 points in 29 minutes against Indiana and sat out the fourth quarter. He hit 14 threes in 27 minutes in Chicago, which is still the franchise record, and he once went 10-for-11 from deep against the Lakers.

Not counting Steph and Klay, the record is 6-3. Two of those losses belong to D'Angelo Russell, who hit nine threes against Dallas on Dec. 28, 2019 and nine more against Indiana on Jan. 24, 2020, and lost both. The Dallas game was a 20-point loss, still the worst in the whole dataset. That's the most 2019-20 Warriors thing imaginable, and I say that with love for everyone who suffered through that season.

Poole went 1-1 and Wiggins went 2-0. Podziemski went 1-0 against the Lakers in April 2025, and Moody went 1-0 last November in New Orleans when he hit seven threes in one quarter and joined Steph and Klay as the only Warriors ever to do it.

A 6-3 record for the non-Splash Brothers isn't a big enough sample to call it a new formula, and one bench explosion against Sacramento doesn't change the math from the last few years. These days the shooting is sometimes the only thing keeping the Warriors in the game.

That's why Wednesday night felt so good. Steph was in street clothes nursing a torn oblique, somebody else got to be the reason an opposing coach was staring at the ceiling wondering what he did to deserve this.

#2607. Egor Demin’s standout outing leaves Nets wanting more

TORONTO — To say the Nets have had a disappointing start to the season would be an understatement.

But on Thanksgiving, the Nets can at least be happy about struggling Egor Dëmin having a bounce-back performance. Probably the best outing of his heretofore underwhelming campaign.

"The guys off the bench, Egor, Noah [Clowney], they were amazing," coach Jordi Fernández said after the Nets' slump-busting victory in Milwaukee.

The Nets snapped their five-game skid that had been tied for the worst in the NBA. And Dëmin showed promising signs of snapping out of his own not-unrelated malaise, coming into Friday's game in Toronto.

Perhaps most auspicious was the fact that it wasn't just a hot shooting showing, but an all-around night.

Part of Dëmin's allure as the eighth overall pick was his size, a 6-foot-9 guard who could not just space the floor but rebound and use his wingspan on defense.

That's happened all too infrequently so far. But it did Wednesday against the Bucks.

Dëmin finished with 15 points, four assists, three rebounds and a game-high plus-15. And despite being 0-for-5 from deep, Dëmin — who has struggled horribly inside the arc — was 5-for-6 from 2-point range. He even added feisty defense.

For a player too often faced with the question of "What can he do but shoot?" this was the answer. One that has to get repeated, starting against the Raptors.

Egor Dëmin, who scored 15 points in the Nets' win over the Bucks, drives past Ryan Rollins during the victory. AP

"Yes, he went back to the simple things and started with this physicality on defense," Fernández said. "They felt him the whole game, his length. Then he can rebound. He can be in the gaps. And then offensively, just simple.

"And I know he's capable of [hitting] every shot. Every 3 that he takes, I think it's going in. He was 0-for-5, but guess what? I think all his shots were great. So that's the way I want him to play: with energy, touching the paint, chasing the ball with his teammates, four assists. Proud of him, for sure."

Three games ago, Fernández had pulled Dëmin from the starting lineup for the first time since November of his rookie campaign.

Egor Dëmin rises up for a layup during the Nets' win over the Bucks in Milwaukee. Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images

Dëmin went into Milwaukee having averaged 11.6 points on just 32.2 percent shooting over his prior five games.

And his woes were the worst on the other end of the court, posting a horrid 137.9 defensive rating during that skid. Dëmin was an aggregate minus-57, with Fernández admitting the Russian needed to be better in terms of his physicality.

Dëmin acknowledged a need to improve and did so against the Bucks. His defensive engagement helped spark a game-changing third-quarter spurt and helped the Nets run — his blown dunk notwithstanding.

"Before anything else, I've got to be present mentally for this team, especially because I'm trying to step in front as a leader role, and help Julius [Randle] out from that standpoint — from that kind of perspective — and help Mike [Porter Jr.] and older guys out with the leadership role," Dëmin said.

"So first off, I've got to be in my own mind out there present, and enjoy the game. And for me, it all came from the defensive side of the game. I was locked in with that, and everything else came to me naturally. Because we were getting stops and getting in transition — not counting that missed dunk — but we were getting wide-open opportunities that we were able to execute."

Dëmin had a block and a steal in the same game for the first time this season. He had three deflections and got in passing lanes.

And when Dëmin checked in with 5:16 left in the third and the Nets down 65-60, he helped ignite a 13-2 run. He had five points and two assists in just 1 ¹/₂ minutes, giving them the lead for good.

"Everybody was able to just put their minds together and not just focus on team defense but their own island, how we say 'guard your yard,' " Dëmin said. "That's where it came from."

The next goal is for Dëmin and the Nets not to lose it before Friday's game in Toronto.

#2606. Bournemouth make history! Marco Rose's men set unprecedented English record in Europe after comeback win over Celta Vigo

Bournemouth's fairy-tale start to life in continental competition reached new heights on Thursday night as they secured a historic victory on Spanish soil. Marco Rose's side showed incredible resilience to overcome both a goal deficit and a first-half red card to maintain their flawless record in the Europa League.

Iago Aspas curled Celta Vigo ahead before Bafode Diakite saw red in the 24th minute for a poorly timed tackle, leaving the visitors a goal and a player down at half-time. Despite playing over an hour with 10 men, Bournemouth controlled the game after the interval.

Amine Adli crossed early in the second half for Alvaro Rodriguez to head an equaliser, before substitute Rayan swept in the winner 12 minutes from time to seal a 2-1 victory.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Adli praised his side's resilience in Spain. "We showed a lot of character," he said. "It's amazing to come back in this way and go back home with the three points."

He also detailed his thinking behind the assist for the equaliser. "I was looking for someone in the box," Adli added. "I know Alvaro is very good in the air and he was in a good position so I just tried to deliver a dangerous ball towards the far post."

Bournemouth are now the first English club to win their opening five European games, and only the third in major continental competitions after Nurnberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73. The triumph also extends their club-record winning run to 10 matches across all competitions, complementing their fifth-place Premier League standing.

Adli credited the squad's half-time belief for driving the turnaround.

"I think it was down to the mentality of the players. From the moment we conceded the goal, and even after the red card, we always believed in ourselves," he noted. "What's fantastic is that in the dressing room, even before the coach started speaking, everybody was saying, 'we can do this.' Everyone was motivated and still believed we could turn things around."

Topping the Europa League league phase table, Bournemouth have one foot in the knockout rounds. Sustaining this unshakeable mentality will be crucial as Rose's men look to safeguard both their European summit and their strong domestic position.

#2605. 10 Eagles things I think I think after incredible comeback vs. Cowboys

There's no other way to describe the Philadelphia Eagles' comeback victory over the Dallas Cowboys — which was way more enjoyable than any meal you could consume on Thanksgiving. This is an Eagles game that's going to be remembered forever, just like the Christmas Day win over the Cowboys in 2006 and the Miracle at the Meadowlands comeback in 2010.

The victory is that improbable, especially when the Eagles were down 31-10 with 3:35 left in the third quarter. They had no business being in this game, yet they found their way back to make it a game — and stole a victory away from the Cowboys on Thanksgiving.

This was a game the Cowboys should have won handily. Instead they choked it away, thanks to the hands of a resilient Eagles team that didn't let their 3-7 record stand in the way of what seemed to be an insurmountable deficit.

No matter how the rest of this season goes, that was one heck of a win. This victory will be talked about amongst generations of Eagles fans.

A Thanksgiving miracle — that may have ended the Cowboys season. The Eagles are good at ruining seasons all of a sudden.

Milton delivered one of the greatest performances my a quarterback in Eagles history. What Milton did against the Cowboys was absolutely incredible, and this was more than a quarterback showing off his ridiculous arm talent.

The final stat line: 21-of-31, 311 yards, 3 TD, 1 INT, 10.7 YPA — 121.8 rating. 3 carries, 15 yards, TD.

There are only two quarterbacks in Eagles history with 300+ passing yards, 3+ passing TD, 1+ rushing TD, and average 10+ YPA in a game — Milton and Michael Vick (2010 at Commanders). That's how well Milton played on Thanksgiving — in just his third career start.

Once the Eagles trailed 31-10, Milton went 11-of-16 for 181 yards with 2 TD, 1 INT and a 120.1 rating (averaging 11.3 YPA). He also had 15 yards and a rushing touchdown in that stretch to bring the Eagles back from three scores.

This level of play was throughout the game. Milton used his arm strength to keep the Eagles offense moving, going 11-of-19 for 278 yards with 3 TD, 1 INT and 14.6 YPA on throws that traveled 10+ air yards — finishing with a 120.1 passer rating. He was 2-of-6 for 95 yards and 2 TD with 0 INT for a 121.5 passer rating on throws that traveled 25+ air yards. Any completion on passes that traveled 25+ air yards was a touchdown.

The Eagles had some exciting performances from Jalen Hurts over the years, but that was arguably the most exciting passing performance by a quarterback since Nick Foles threw for 471 yards against the Houston Texans in 2018 (and that was an Eagles' win too).

Impressive performance by Milton, finally giving life to an Eagles offense that badly needed it.

Milton had a touchdown pass that traveled 64.4 yards in air distance, and that wasn't the most impressive aspect of his performance. He threw an interception into triple coverage with 7:14 to play when the Eagles were trailing 38-3, which seemed to be the backbreaker with how the defense was playing.

The Eagles got the ball back and Milton goes 4-of-4 for 70 yards and a 24-yard touchdown to Makai lemon on the ensuing drive — netting a perfect 158.3 passer rating. The poise and ability to forget that interception immediately following the interception spoke more volumes about who Milton is as a player than anything else he accomplished on Thanksgiving.

When Milton made a boneheaded play, he responded in the way winning quarterbacks respond. He hasn't even been on his team for two months and was able to shake that play off and perform at an even higher level.

Since the interception, Milton finished 6-of-9 for 84 yards with a touchdown and a 133.6 passer rating. He led the Eagles to victory with a touchdown drive and set Jake Elliott up with his game-winning field goal.

Want to know how to stick around as a starting quarterback in the NFL? Moments like that.

One of the few things I wanted to see in the remainder of the season was if Milton could play well enough to be the QB2 next year. Judging Milton through two starts was tough, given the state of the offense and the changes the Eagles were making to accomondate his game.

Milton didn't get to throw the deep ball much, and he missed when he had his opportunity last week to DeVonta Smith. He didn't miss any of those opportunities on Thanksgiving, hitting two of them for 95 yards and two touchdowns.

On throws that traveled 20+ air yards, Milton went 6-of-11 for 188 yards and 3 TD with 0 INT — a 139.2 passer rating. The arm strength was clearly on display, along with the accuracy on the deep ball.

Milton was relentless facing pressure too, finishing 7-of-10 for 154 yards with 3 TD and 0 INT for a 152.1 passer rating — while also being sacked five times. He was 6-of-8 for 145 yards with 3 TD and 0 INT on throws from outside the pocket — 156.3 rating.

Backup quarterbacks don't have games like this. QB5's — which is what Milton was when he signed — really don't have games like this.

This performance may have locked up QB2 for Milton next year. If Milton can stack up good-to-solid performances, he'll be the QB2 on the Eagles (at least).

Milton may get a starting opportunity elsewhere too (he is a restricted free agent), but the Eagles can control his fate there as well. The situation needs to play itself out, but Milton is certainly on the radar around the league.

When Milton was making incredible throws against the Cowboys, I couldn't help but think of his journey to get to this point. Over the last four months, Milton was cut by the Cowboys after losing the QB2 job to Sam Howell —toiling on the practice squad for five weeks.

Any team could have claimed Milton when he was waived, and no team did. Any team could have signed Milton from the Cowboys practice squad to the active roster, and no one did.

The Eagles signed Milton to the active roster when Jalen Hurts was lost for the season due to blood clots in his lungs. If Hurts wasn't done for the year, the Eagles wouldn't have brought in Milton.

He literally was their QB5, the fifth quarterback to make the active roster. Tanner McKee got three starts before the Eagles turned to Milton, Andy Dalton told the Eagles he had a better opportunity with the Atlanta Falcons.

Milton wasn't considered by the Cowboys and 31 other teams until the Eagles needed a quarterback. To have a performance like that against a team that cut him and chose Sam Howell over him had to be bittersweet — especially since he led the Eagles to a 21-point comeback on the road against that team on Thanksgiving in just his third start.

Certainly Milton will soak that all in at some point, but the battle to succeed and have a moment like that are why sports are so great. Even when Milton was counted out, he wasn't.

There were questions whether DeVonta Smith was a WR1 earlier this season. There shouldn't be any following Thanksgiving.

Smith finished with 11 catches for 200 yards and two touchdowns in the win over the Cowboys, the first Eagles' player to get 200+ receiving yards in a game since DeSean Jackson in 2010. He had the most receiving yards on Thanksgiving since 1945 — and the second-most by any player on the holiday in NFL history.

Smith had two touchdown catches of 45+ yards, the first player to do that on Thanksgiving since Randy Moss in 1998. He had more receiving yards on Thanksgiving (200) than A.J. Brown has the whole season (128).

How good was the Milton-Smith connection? Milton was 11-of-14 for 200 yards with 2 TD, 0 INT and a 158.3 passer rating when targeting Smith — 14.3 yards per attempt. He hit Smith on throws of 24, 50, 45, and 23 yards of those 11 completions, and also hit him six times on throws of 10+ air yards.

When Smith is healthy, he's very good. He wasn't even fully healthy in this one, injuring his lower back trying to make an insane catch in the fourth quarter on a Milton deep ball. Smith could barely run at full speed the rest of the way, yet still was able to go out and make plays.

Smith has 42 catches for 551 yards and 4 TD in six games. He's averaging 91.8 receiving yards per game, a 17-game pace of 1,561 yards. With the injuries, Smith is still on pace for 851 receiving yards (and those numbers will go up if he's good enough to play).

Milton has an excellent chance to stick around with Smith on the field. That connection was brilliant on Thanksgiving.

Hard to state the claim the Eagles have given up on Nick Sirianni based on the last two games.

A win against the Pittsburgh Steelers to end a seven-game losing streak is a gut-check victory. Stealing a game on Thanksgiving against the Dallas Cowboys is in unchartered territory.

The Eagles were down 21 points with 3:35 left in the third quarter. They had eight plays in the quarter that went for 1 yard at that point, while the defense allowed 31 points on seven possessions and 6.7 yards per play.

They could have packed it in and allowed Dallas to continue to roll. They didn't.

The Eagles not giving up in a season that has experienced injury after injury (including the multiple starters that left the game), team captains and long-time starters getting traded, the handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots, and the uncertain future of the coaching staff speaks volumes of how Nick Sirianni prepares his team during the week.

No matter what Sirianni does during a game (and after), his players are still playing for him. The message is still getting across to the players in that locker room and the Eagles don't believe their playoff chances are dead yet.

If Sirianni is back after this season, this is the reason why. This locker room has no checked out on him, and they are demonstrating that with their performance on the field.

Any team could have called it a day down 31-10 late in the third quarter. Not the Eagles, who had their biggest comeback in 16 years.

I understand why Sirianni acts like he does. Sirianni is a very emotional individual and a competitor who puts his heart and soul into coaching.

Going on a seven-game losing streak took its toll on Sirianni, who spent weeks trying to figure out what was going on with his football team. This is a head coach who was 59-26 (.694 win percetatge) after his first five seasons, making the playoffs all five years and winning a Super Bowl while appearing in another one.

Sirianni is fighting for his team — and his job. The last two months have been brutal.

The Eagles head coach gets caught up in the moment with fans a little too much. He lets his emotions get the best of him. I'm not even sure if he was interacting with Eagles fans or taunting Cowboys fans, but it was enough where he had to be pulled away by Dom DiSandro.

Sirianni shouldn't be putting himself in that situation, and he's done it far too much. I like that he's authentic, but that is taking it too far.

The Eagles head coach shouldn't care what the fans think of him, good or bad. It's clear Sirianni hears what's said of him and acts on it when he wins.

Sirianni gets over the top with this stuff, a silly distraction after the massive win. The Eagles have enough issues to worry about inside the Jefferson Health Training Complex.

Can't speak enough on how good Jake Elliott has been all season. Elliott's two field goals on Sunday were the reason the Eagles won, and he gave the Eagles their first lead of the game on a 59-yard field goal with two seconds left — and the kick would have been good from 65 yards.

Elliott had ice in his veins when making that kick, just like the majority of clutch kicks he's made in his career. Elliott is 14-of-14 on field goals in the final minute of a game in regulation or overtime, 5-of-5 on kicks of 50+ yards in one-score games.

He's 2-for-2 in those situations this season, and 1-of-1 on game-winning field goals.

Elliott has improved to 5-of-5 on 50+ yard field goal attempts, after being 5-of-15 (33.3%) on those kicks over the previous two seasons. Elliott is 8-of-9 (88.9%) on 40+ yard kicks this season after going 20-of-34 (58.9%) on those kicks over the previous two seasons.

The comeback is incredible, and why the Eagles chose to adamantly defend Elliott this offseason. Just an amazing season from Elliott, who might be in line for an All-Pro campaign.

This Eagles comeback doesn't happen without Robinson, who made the most of his opportunity when his number was called. Robinson had three pressures in seven pass-rushing snaps, an insane pressure rate of 42.9%.

One of those pressures was the fourth-down sack on Dak Prescott on 4th-and-1 with 55 seconds left — the first one of Robinson's career. This was a player who wasn't even guaranteed to make the roster once training camp started, and earned his way onto this team with his play in training camp.

That play set the Eagles up to steal the game, and set off a fire in Dallas on whether Brian Schottenheimer should have punted or went for it — enough where his job is in question. Robinson was able to make that massive of a presence as a pass rusher, and deserves more playing time going forward.

Oh, and Robinson also blocked a punt that was recovered by Kenny Moore for a touchdown. That play was massive in the Eagles' comeback, and cut the deficit to 31-24 with 13:53 left in the game. Robinson should have been credited with a forced fumble in this game too, but I digress.

Robinson is the first player in Eagles history to record a sack and a blocked punt in the same game. This is a player that logged just 73 defensive snaps this season prior to Thursday.

The Eagles have something with Robinson. They traded Jordan Davis for multiple reasons.

The Eagles entered this game with the worst second-half offense in football. The 4.6 point average in the second half was last in the NFL. So was the yards per play (3.6), average yards in second half (110.1), and net yards per attempt (4.3). The only major statistic that wasn't 32nd was yards per carry — 30th at 3.3.

This week was significantly different. The Eagles scored 22 offensive points in the second half (29 total), averaging 6.9 yards per play and gaining 200 yards of offense. They averaged 5.4 yards per carry and 8.5 net yards per attempt — all this while only converting 20% of third downs.

This was the worst team in football in the second half, and they're still last in the league in offensive points scored (6.2), yards per play (3.9), and average yards in second half (118.3). yards per carry moved up to 29th (3.4) and net yards per attempt improved to 31st (4.8).

The Eagles even scored in the third quarter! Milton's touchdown pass in the third quarter was just the second touchdown scored by the Eagles in the third quarter all season — the other one was against the Cowboys. They improved their third quarter scoring average to 30th in the league (2.1 points).

This offense in the second half underwent a complete 180, and it didn't start out that way (first eight plays went for a yard). Amazing turnaround once Milton hit Smith on that 45-yard touchdown with 24 seconds left in the third quarter.

Can the Eagles build off this? Hopefully.

Bonus: Enjoy this win (enjoy all of them). This is one the city of Philadelphia will talk about for a long time, even better since this season has been a disaster and this matchup seemed like a easy victory for the Cowboys (I didn't even think the Eagles could score 20 points when I was watching Dallas film on Monday).

You'll remember where you were and who you were with when the Eagles pulled off this comeback.

The Eagles are 4-0 against the Cowboys on Thanksgiving and Christmas — all games in Dallas. Happy Thanksgiving everyone!

#2603. 'You're always allowed to dream' - Marco Rose backs Bournemouth's Europa League ambitions after 10-man comeback against Celta Vigo seals 10th straight victory

Bournemouth manager Marco Rose has backed his side's Europa League ambitions after a stunning 10-man comeback against Celta Vigo sealed a club-record 10th straight victory on Thursday. Despite Bafode Diakite's early red card, the Cherries fought back to win 2-1 in Spain and maintain their perfect start to their debut European campaign.

Bournemouth overcame a first-half deficit and a red card to extend their winning streak in Spain. Iago Aspas had curled Celta ahead before Bafode Diakite was dismissed via VAR in the 23rd minute for catching Couhaib Driouech high on the ankle. Second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and substitute Rayan then turned the match around as Celta saw three strikes ruled out for offside.

The dramatic turnaround left Bournemouth top of the Europa League table with five wins from five, becoming only the third side to win their opening five major European fixtures after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73. Already rated among the tournament favourites with a 26 per cent title chance by the Opta supercomputer before kick-off, Rose refused to dampen expectations.

Speaking to TNT Sports, Rose said: "You're always allowed to dream. If you get into a competition like this, you want to achieve the best possible things, but we know that there's a long way to go, with many games.

"Now it's about getting in the top eight, to avoid even more games for us, as a Premier League club, and then we can see, step by step. Staying humble is good in our situation, and working hard."

Thursday's triumph made Bournemouth the first Premier League team in any competition to win after trailing with 10 men at half-time since Liverpool beat Newcastle United in August 2023. Remarkably, Rose made eight changes from their previous league outing, yet his side improved after the dismissal, firing seven second-half shots compared to three before the interval.

Momentum shifted when Rodriguez headed in Amine Adli's inswinging cross, before fellow substitutes Adrien Truffert and Marcus Tavernier combined to set up Rayan's winner. It caps an extraordinary revival for Andoni Iraola's successor, who sat just above the relegation zone without a league win after losing 5-1 to Chelsea on October 10, only to reel off 10 straight wins while scoring at least twice in every game.

Rose now faces another rapid turnaround as fifth-placed Bournemouth travel to Fulham on Sunday in the Premier League. Sitting just four points off second place, the Cherries will be eager to carry their relentless momentum back into domestic action. Securing another victory in west London would keep their remarkable winning streak alive while easing the pressure of juggling European and league commitments.

#2602. Game Preview: Knicks vs. Heat, November 27, 2026

Back in the 1990s, one way to preserve basketball games for the future was to record them on a VHS cassette. For all the younger folks, this was a big, chunky, rectangular thing that had magnetic tape on the inside. Whenever a game was on TV, you popped your cassette into the video recorder, pressed "REC," and from that point on, you could rewatch anything you recorded whenever you wanted. Or for as long as the tape held up, for that matter.

My favorite recorded event back then was Game Five of the first round of the playoffs in 1999 between your New York Knicks and the Miami Heat. It ended with Allan Houston's historic leaning jumper with 0.8 seconds to go, sending the top-seeded team coached by the Godfather of Schenectady packing and the underdog Bockers on an improbable run all the way to the NBA Finals. The tape wasn't just special to me because of the historic shot or the basketball played with bad intentions back then. It was also awesome because it showed the Knicks beating the Heat. Sorry, Grandma, I know you taught me not to hate anyone, but those were the Heat, my favorite team's biggest rival for years.

Now, before A'ja Wilson's boyfriend thinks he can hold a candle to the guy Patrick Ewing once offered one of his kidneys to, let me make it clear: That was a different time, a different rivalry. Whoever experienced it firsthand knows what I mean by that. When the Knicks meet the Heat on Friday night for their fourth NBA Cup game of the season, it will be different, much different. Different players, different coaches. Heck, it all seems like a different world. But make no mistake about it—it's still Knicks versus Heat. Which means the stakes are just a bit higher than in a game versus the magicians from the nation's capital or the royalty from "The Big Tomato."

Friday's game will be particularly interesting because it gives the Knicks a first glimpse at the newest version of the Heat, featuring Greece's national hero Giannis Antetokounmpo, who also happens to be one of the greatest and probably most unique basketball players this generation has seen. The project started pretty badly, with Giannis continuously reminding everyone who cared and everyone who didn't that he dearly missed Milwaukee, the city he had called home for every second of his storied NBA career until then. Then the schematic issues befell the not-so-hot Heat, who struggled with spacing, players playing in new roles, and the daunting task of implementing a headstrong player with immense gravity into a completely new system. Defense? Haha, good one!

But after a 3-6 start, the second-oldest team in the league decided this wasn't the way to ride off into the sunset. Or rather, their famous coach made plenty of adjustments. Erik Spoelstra, as we all know, is one of the best in the business. Not only at taking average rosters into the Play-In Tournament but indeed at coaching that sport with the orange leather. He inserted young Pelle Larsson into the starting lineup, found a spacing solution for the Heat, doubled down on their identity as a full-court, offensive-minded team, and then watched his guys reel off seven mostly impressive victories in a row (among them wins over Houston and Detroit) before falling to Philly on Wednesday night.

What can we expect from the Heat specifically? They love to get up and down the court and play at the third-highest pace in the entire league. Currently, only the Memphis Grizzlies score more points than Spoelstra's squad, and the Heat do it by shooting a high percentage from the field, drawing boatloads of fouls, and making use of two post players. Yes, you read that right—post players. Both Giannis and A'ja Wilson's boyfriend can effectively score with their backs to the basket, and despite many worries, they can actually coexist next to one another. One of them fills the dunker spot almost all the time, they rotate decisively in screen actions, and overall, Miami runs its sets fast and ferociously to get them rolling downhill. They don't just set screens to see where it leads them; they want to get into an action quickly before any lanes can close.

It works, partly because the players around Giannis and that guy who made a habit last year of disliking the team that won a championship before him are all doing a good job in their roles. Klay Thompson adds shooting (43.2 percent from downtown), Swedish Swiss Army knife Pelle Larsson provides a little bit of everything, and playmaker Davion Mitchell has all of a sudden turned into one of the better point guards in the league at age 28, averaging career highs of 17 points and 8.6 assists per contest while also shooting 51 percent from the floor and 43-plus percent from behind the arc. The bench has some older vets more or less collecting paychecks so far, but Bobby Portis and Andrew Wiggins clearly have some talent. Apparently, that also describes Ryan Conwell, a stocky second-round guard who has been a pleasant surprise for Miami.

That whole group will definitely look to waltz into Madison Square Garden on Friday with the idea of showing the champs that they are a team to be reckoned with. Whether they truly are remains to be seen; there are plenty of things that could uproot the positivity currently sprawling across South Beach. But the Knicks better be prepared for a tough test, and not because they might still be missing some of their injured guys or because they are coming off an emotionally draining victory against Cleveland on Wednesday. Not even because A'ja Wilson might have taught her boyfriend a few more tricks this offseason after winning her fifth WNBA MVP trophy.

No, it's going to be tough because it's Heat versus Knicks. And even if that doesn't mean what it did in the days of the VHS cassette, it still means something.

#2600. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

The New York Mets and center fielder A.J. Ewing have agreed to an eight-year contract extension, SNY reports. The deal will pay Ewing a guaranteed $95 million and includes an option for a ninth year, according to The Athletic. The extension will run through the 2034 season and, if the option is exercised, through 2035.

Ewing, 22, is coming off a 2026 rookie campaign in which he batted .252/.324/.376 (97 OPS+) with 11 home runs and 25 stolen bases in 120 games for the Mets. Additionally, Ewing graded out as a pronounced defensive asset in center field according to the eye test and fielding metrics. His overall WAR of 3.1 this past season helped him crack the top 10 in the National League Rookie of the Year vote.

The Mets originally selected Ewing in the fourth round of the 2023 draft out of an Ohio high school. Following a strong campaign at Double-A and Triple-A in 2025, Ewing entered the 2026 season as a consensus top-100 prospect in baseball. In terms of overall value, he's already begun living up to those expectations.

The extension expresses confidence on the club's side that Ewing will continue to be a valuable core contributor for years to come. Even if the bat doesn't develop as hoped, Ewing's foundation of excellent defense at an up-the-middle position provides him a high floor of worth over the long term. He's part of an emerging core of young Mets talent that also includes starting pitcher Nolan McLean and Ewing's fellow outfielder Carson Benge, who both finished ahead of Ewing in that Rookie of the Year balloting. As well, catcher Francisco Alvarez is still just 25 years old.

No matter what happens with the Mets' high ambitions on the free-agent market, Ewing will be an essential part of the Mets' efforts to move beyond the disappointments of 2026. This past season, the Mets finished 14 games below .500 and in last place in the NL East despite having the league's highest Opening Day payroll.

Mike Brown reacts on the sidelines during the Knicks' win over the Cavaliers on Nov. 25, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for New York Post
